name: Common Corpus
description: Common Corpus is the largest open dataset for language model pre-training, containing about two trillion tokens of data that are either uncopyrighted or under permissible licenses. The dataset contains a wide variety of languages, ranging from the main European languages to low-resource ones rarely present in pre-training datasets, and includes a large portion of code data. The diversity of data sources in terms of covered domains and time periods opens up paths for both research and entrepreneurial needs in diverse areas of knowledge.
license: Mixed: Public Domain, CC-By, MIT, CC-By-SA, Apache-2.0, BSD-3-Clause, Open license, BSD-2-Clause, CC-BY-4.0, CC0-1.0
creator: PleIAs, Paris, France
inLanguage: Multilingual (English, French, German, Spanish, Latin, Italian, Polish, Greek, Portuguese, Russian, and many others)
citeAs: Pierre-Carl Langlais, Carlos Rosas Hinostroza, Mattia Nee, Catherine Arnett, Pavel Chizhov, Eliot Krzystof Jones, Irène Girard, David Mach, Anastasia Stasenko, Ivan P. Yamshchikov. Common Corpus: The Largest Collection of Ethical Data for LLM Pre-Training. arXiv:2506.01732v1 [cs.CL] 2 Jun 2025
rai:dataCollection: Common Corpus was assembled from multiple sources including web archives, cultural heritage institutions, government databases, scientific repositories, and code repositories. The data collection process involved aggregating data from Collections As Data (CAD) initiatives, using APIs and standard retrieval methods, and implementing resource-by-resource collection. The collection began in May 2023 as a French corpus and expanded to become a multilingual dataset by 2024-2025.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Web API, Secondary Data analysis, Software Collection, Document analysis, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Data sources include: (1) Open Government: SEC annual reports (1993-2024), WTO documents (1995-2024), French AMF documents, EU TED procurement notices, GATT Library documents (1946-1996), Europarl proceedings, Caselaw Access Project, CourtListener, EUR-lex, Eurovoc, French administrative data, USPTO documents (2019-2022), UN Digital Library, OECD data; (2) Open Culture: Chronicle America newspapers, Europeana newspapers, Gallica (French National Library), Biblioteca (Spanish), Library of Congress books, New Zealand Papers Past, German Digital Library newspapers, various European national libraries; (3) Open Science: OpenAlex scientific papers, arXiv, HAL, and other open access repositories; (4) Open Code: Stack v1 and v2 from GitHub; (5) Open Web: Wikipedia, Wikisource, YouTube Commons transcripts, StackExchange; (6) Open Semantic: Wikidata.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: Data collection began in May 2023 and continued through February 2025. The collected documents span from 1618 to 2024, with different collections covering different time periods.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Data manipulation included: (1) Text segmentation using Segmentext model to handle broken and unstructured texts with digitization artifacts; (2) OCR correction using OCRonos model based on Llama 3 8B to correct OCR errors, wrong word cuts or merges, and broken text structures; (3) License filtering to retain only permissible licenses; (4) Format filtering to remove non-informative file types; (5) Replacement of sequences of [\r]+\n with \n and recalculation of line lengths.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Preprocessing steps included: (1) OCR error detection using OCRoscope and OCRerrcr tools to determine digitization quality; (2) Text segmentation using Segmentext model trained to be resilient to broken and unstructured texts; (3) OCR correction using OCRonos for highly deteriorated content; (4) PII removal using Microsoft's Presidio with custom regular expression patterns, replacing PII with fictitious but realistic values; (5) Toxicity filtering using Celadon classifier to identify and remove harmful content along five dimensions (race/origin bias, gender/sexuality bias, religious bias, ability bias, violence/abuse); (6) For code data: removal of files not in desired languages/formats, license filtering, manual filters for low-quality data, removal of files with 75%+ digits; (7) Language identification using fastText; (8) Rights verification for cultural heritage content based on author life + 70 years, publication dates, and copyright terms.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Segmentext (text segmentation model), OCRoscope (OCR quality detection based on cld2), OCRerrcr (DeBERTa-v2-style language model with 400M parameters for OCR error detection), OCRonos (Llama 3 8B-based model for OCR correction), Microsoft's Presidio (PII detection and removal), Celadon (DeBERTa-v3-small multilingual toxicity classifier with ~140M parameters), fastText (language identification), cld2 (language identification)
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: Common Corpus is an evolving resource reflecting the need for continuous open infrastructure rather than a fixed dataset. HuggingFace ensures proper archiving of past versions for reproducibility. The dataset was first released in March 2024, with additional releases throughout 2024, a unified corpus release in November 2024, and the current version released in February 2025 for the Paris AI Summit. Future collection of permissible data is planned, including expansion of corpora in African languages (e.g., Swahili, Wolof, Bambara) as part of the LLMs4EU project.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset originally contained PII including phone numbers, email addresses, and IP addresses. PII was identified and removed using Microsoft's Presidio with custom regular expression patterns. Instead of removing or tagging PII, it was replaced with fictitious but realistic values to maintain text format and model understanding.
rai:dataSocialImpact: Common Corpus addresses legal uncertainties that have significantly impeded the development of open science research on LLMs. It provides truly open pre-training data compliant with data security regulations, particularly EU AI regulations. The dataset enables the development of fully open and auditable LLMs without relying on fair use provisions. It supports multilingual model development, reducing the restriction of open-data language models to English-speaking audiences. The dataset has been used by industry leaders like Anthropic and multiple LLM training projects, becoming critical infrastructure for open science research in LLMs.
rai:dataBiases: Historical texts in Open Culture (from 18th-19th centuries or earlier) may not meet modern ethical standards regarding discussion of certain ethnic groups, women, and themes such as violence. To address this, a toxicity filtering pipeline was implemented using the Celadon classifier to identify documents containing harmful language along five dimensions: race and origin-based bias, gender and sexuality-based bias, religious bias, ability bias, and violence and abuse. Documents with harmful content are either removed or synthetically rewritten.
rai:dataLimitations: Known limitations include: (1) The dataset does not collect the whole range of available open data (open data paradox); (2) Coverage for low-resource languages is still shallow despite large language diversity; (3) The amount of collected data (2 trillion tokens) is suitable for pre-training models of limited size but larger models will require significantly larger amounts of data; (4) The dataset does not contain data for instruction-tuning or specialized tasks, making it not directly suitable for task-specific fine-tuning; (5) Curation methods (OCR correction, toxicity detection, PII removal) cannot facilitate hundred-percent accuracy; (6) OCR errors present in some data may pose challenges to models; (7) Major sources of open content are paradoxically little visible online and in leading sources currently used for pre-training.
rai:dataUseCases: Dataset uses include: (1) Training: Pre-training of language models, including the Pleias 1.0 family (350M, 1.2B, 3B parameters), Salamandra series (2B, 7B, 40B parameters), Lucie 7B, and others; (2) Testing and Validation: Used in evaluations for retrieval augmented generation (Pleias-RAG models); (3) Fine-tuning: NeKo language correction model used OCR-corrected parts for training and evaluation; (4) Creating new datasets: YouTube Commons used to create FineVideo and Mosel multimodal datasets; (5) Research: Feature visualization experiments by Anthropic; (6) Development of multilingual language models with diverse and creative writing styles; (7) Historical language model development using temporal metadata; (8) Coding applications and improving model performance on reasoning, world knowledge, mathematics, and structured output tasks. Usage guidelines emphasize legal compliance with AI regulations, particularly EU regulations, and adherence to open-source AI definitions.
